title: Five substitutes are handing the title to the richest squads

defects.quote: The back-pass rule, introduced in 1998, stopped goalkeepers picking the ball up from a team-mate's pass
defects.correction: The back-pass rule was introduced in 1992.
defects.note: [secondary-source] Top results are likely fan sites and news retrospectives; the primary source is the IFAB Laws of the Game and its 1992 amendment.

defects.quote: English football switched to three points for a win in 1981, and FIFA followed at the 1990 World Cup
defects.correction: FIFA first used three points for a win at the 1994 World Cup (the 1981 date for English football is correct).
defects.note: [multi-part] The first half of the quote (England switched to three points for a win in 1981) is true; only the World Cup year is wrong.

defects.quote: Since the five-substitute rule arrived, the richest six clubs have won 12% more points from losing positions than they did before.
Bigger squads benefit most from five substitutes, therefore the rule exists only to help the rich clubs.
defects.known_rebuttal: Who benefits does not establish why a rule exists. Five substitutes were introduced in 2020 as a temporary answer to fixture congestion after the pandemic shutdown and made permanent by IFAB in 2022 on player-welfare grounds, and Premier League clubs, including the richest, at first voted to go back to three before adopting five from 2022-23. Smaller clubs also use the extra changes to protect thin squads from injury, so the effect on competitive balance is an empirical question, not proof of intent.
